about: Digital Circuits and Information Processing is a 16-lecture Part IA course in the Cambridge Engineering Tripos, part of 1P3 and examined in Paper 3 (Electrical and Information Engineering), one of four 3-hour Part IA exams (per the 2025-26 course structure page). This pack follows the Department's syllabus page (last modified December 2023 and still the current page when checked in October 2026): logic gates and families, Boolean algebra, Karnaugh maps, hazards and VHDL, then number codes, flip-flops, counters, state-machine design, D/A conversion and arithmetic circuits, then microprocessor architecture, memory and address decoding, and PIC12F629/675 assembly programming. The pack places arithmetic circuits with number codes rather than at the end of the sequential-logic section. It is supported by a 4-period PIC programming and analogue-interfacing experiment and short logic experiments.
topics: Logic gates and logic families (NMOS and CMOS)
Gate delays, timing diagrams, hazards and VHDL
Number codes and binary arithmetic circuits
Counters, shift registers and serial communication
Microprocessor architecture, memory and address decoding
PIC programming and the PIC12F629/675 instruction set

notes.body:
Digital circuits represent information with two voltage ranges, read as logic 0 and logic 1. In positive logic the higher voltage is 1. The first lectures revise the basic gates and then look inside them.

The basic gates
- NOT: output is the complement of the input.
- AND: 1 only if all inputs are 1. OR: 1 if any input is 1.
- NAND and NOR: AND and OR followed by NOT. Each is universal: any Boolean function can be built from NAND gates alone (or NOR gates alone).
- XOR: 1 when an odd number of inputs are 1 (for two inputs, when they differ). XNOR is its complement and acts as an equality detector.

Voltage levels and noise margins
A gate does not need a perfect 0 V or supply voltage; it needs a level inside the right band.
- VOH(min) and VOL(max): the worst-case high and low output voltages a gate guarantees.
- VIH(min) and VIL(max): the input voltages a gate is guaranteed to read as 1 and 0.
- Noise margins: NMH = VOH(min) − VIH(min) and NML = VIL(max) − VOL(max). For standard 74-series TTL, VOH(min) = 2.4 V, VIH(min) = 2.0 V, VIL(max) = 0.8 V, VOL(max) = 0.4 V, so both margins are 0.4 V.
- Inputs between VIL(max) and VIH(min) are undefined, which is why slow or noisy signals cause trouble (see Schmitt triggers).

Logic families
- TTL uses bipolar transistors; it was the classic 74-series family.
- NMOS logic uses n-channel MOSFETs pulling the output down against a load (a resistor or a transistor acting as one). When the output is low, current flows continuously from the supply through the load, so it dissipates static power.
- CMOS uses complementary pairs of p-channel and n-channel MOSFETs. In either steady state one network is off, so almost no static current flows. Power is mainly dynamic, roughly proportional to C·V²·f, so it rises with switching frequency and supply voltage.

CMOS gate circuits
- Inverter: a PMOS from the supply to the output and an NMOS from the output to ground, gates joined to the input. Input high: NMOS on, PMOS off, output low. Input low: the reverse.
- NAND: two PMOS in parallel to the supply, two NMOS in series to ground. The output is pulled low only if both inputs are high.
- NOR: two PMOS in series, two NMOS in parallel.
- The pull-up and pull-down networks are duals: series in one becomes parallel in the other. Because inverting gates fall out naturally, NAND and NOR are the cheapest CMOS gates; AND and OR need an extra inverter.

Other parameters
- Propagation delay: tPLH and tPHL measured between 50% points of input and output.
- Rise and fall times, usually measured between 10% and 90% of the swing.
- Fan-out: how many inputs one output can drive while still meeting its specified levels.

Exam tips: be able to draw the CMOS inverter, NAND and NOR from memory, explain why CMOS has low static power, and calculate noise margins from a table of VOH, VOL, VIH and VIL.

Boolean algebra lets you turn a written requirement into an expression, simplify it and then build it with as few gates as possible. Write A' for NOT A.

Key laws
- Identity and null: A + 0 = A, A·1 = A, A + 1 = 1, A·0 = 0.
- Idempotent and complement: A + A = A, A + A' = 1, A·A' = 0.
- Distributive, including the less familiar form: A + BC = (A + B)(A + C).
- Absorption: A + AB = A, and A + A'B = A + B.
- De Morgan: (A + B)' = A'·B' and (AB)' = A' + B'. In words: break the bar and change the operator.

Standard forms
- Sum of products (SOP): OR of AND terms. A minterm is a product containing every variable once; F = Σm(...) lists the input rows where F = 1.
- Product of sums (POS): AND of OR terms, built from the rows where F = 0 (maxterms).
- From words to logic: "the alarm sounds if at least two of three sensors trip" is the majority function M = AB + BC + AC.

Karnaugh maps
A K-map is the truth table drawn so that neighbouring cells differ in exactly one variable. Rows and columns are labelled in Gray-code order 00, 01, 11, 10, and the map wraps round top to bottom and side to side.
- Loop groups of 1s whose size is a power of two (1, 2, 4, 8).
- Make each group as large as possible, and use as few groups as possible; groups may overlap.
- Each group gives one product term containing only the variables that stay constant across it. A group of 2ᵏ cells removes k variables.
- Don't-care cells (X) are inputs that never occur or whose output does not matter. Include them in a group if that makes it bigger; otherwise ignore them.
- Group 0s instead to get a minimal POS.
The syllabus expects maps with up to four variables.

Worked example
F(A,B,C,D) = Σm(0, 2, 5, 7, 8, 10, 13, 15).
- Cells 0, 2, 8, 10 are the four corners (B = 0, D = 0): one group of four, giving B'D'.
- Cells 5, 7, 13, 15 form a central block (B = 1, D = 1): giving BD.
- So F = B'D' + BD, which is simply B XNOR D. Eight minterms collapse to one gate.

Gate-level implementation
- A two-level SOP maps directly onto NAND–NAND logic: replace both the AND layer and the OR layer by NANDs (by De Morgan, a NAND of NANDs is an OR of ANDs).
- A POS maps onto NOR–NOR logic in the same way.
- If only one gate type is available, as with a single type of chip on a board, this is how you meet the requirement.

Exam tips: always label the K-map axes in Gray-code order, state the groups you chose, and check your simplified expression against two or three rows of the original truth table.

notes.h: Gate delays, timing diagrams, hazards and VHDL
notes.body:
Real gates take time to respond, and this causes behaviour that Boolean algebra alone does not predict.

Propagation delay and timing diagrams
- Each gate has a propagation delay of the order of nanoseconds (tPLH for an output rising, tPHL for falling).
- A timing diagram plots each signal against time. Draw the input changes, then shift each gate's output by its delay.
- Signals that pass through different numbers of gates arrive at different times. If they recombine, the output can briefly take the wrong value. This brief wrong output is called a glitch.

Static hazards
- A static-1 hazard is when the output should stay at 1 but momentarily drops to 0 as an input changes. A static-0 hazard is a momentary 1 when the output should stay at 0.
- Example: F = AC' + BC. With A = B = 1, F = C' + C, which should always be 1. When C falls from 1 to 0, the term BC switches off at once, but C' only rises after the inverter delay, so for a short time both terms are 0 and F glitches low.
- On a K-map the two product terms are adjacent groups that do not overlap. The transition between them is not covered by any single group.
- Cure: add the redundant consensus term AB. Then F = AC' + BC + AB, which is logically the same function, but AB holds the output at 1 throughout the transition. In general, add groups so that every pair of adjacent 1s is covered by a common group.
- Hazards matter most when an output drives something edge-sensitive, such as a clock input or an asynchronous reset.

Introduction to VHDL
VHDL is a hardware description language. You describe a circuit in text, then simulate it, or synthesise it into gates for a programmable device such as an FPGA.
- An entity declares the interface: the input and output ports.
- An architecture describes the behaviour or structure.
- A minimal example for the majority function:
  library ieee; use ieee.std_logic_1164.all;
  entity majority is port (a, b, c : in std_logic; y : out std_logic); end majority;
  architecture rtl of majority is begin y <= (a and b) or (b and c) or (a and c); end rtl;
- Concurrent signal assignments (<=) all act at the same time, like real wires and gates. VHDL is not a sequential program in the way Python is.
- Clocked behaviour is written inside a process: if rising_edge(clk) then q <= d; end if; describes a D flip-flop.

Why use it
- Large designs are impractical to draw gate by gate.
- The same description can be simulated before building, checked automatically and re-targeted to different hardware.
- It documents the design precisely.

Exam tips: be ready to draw a timing diagram showing a glitch, identify a hazard on a K-map and remove it with a consensus term, and read a short piece of VHDL and state the logic it describes.

notes.h: Number codes and binary arithmetic circuits
notes.body:
Bases
- Binary is base 2, octal base 8, hexadecimal base 16 (digits 0–9, A–F).
- Group binary digits in fours for hex and in threes for octal, counting from the right.
- Example: 0xB7 = 1011 0111 = 11 × 16 + 7 = 183. In octal, 10 110 111 = 267₈ = 2 × 64 + 6 × 8 + 7 = 183.
- Decimal to binary: divide repeatedly by 2 and read the remainders from the bottom up.

Other codes
- BCD (binary-coded decimal): each decimal digit in its own 4 bits. 183 = 0001 1000 0011. The patterns 1010 to 1111 are unused.
- ASCII: a 7-bit character code. 'A' = 65 = 0x41, 'a' = 0x61, and the digit '0' = 0x30, so a digit's ASCII code is its value plus 0x30.
- Gray code: successive values differ in exactly one bit (000, 001, 011, 010, 110, 111, 101, 100). It is used in position encoders and K-map labelling because it avoids false intermediate readings. Conversion from binary: each Gray bit is the XOR of a binary bit and the bit above it, g = b XOR (b shifted right by 1).

Signed numbers
- Sign-magnitude: the top bit is the sign. There are two zeros, and adding is awkward.
- One's complement: negate by inverting all bits. There are also two zeros.
- Two's complement: negate by inverting all bits and adding 1. There is one zero, and the same adder works for signed and unsigned numbers.
- An n-bit two's complement number has range −2ⁿ⁻¹ to 2ⁿ⁻¹ − 1. For 8 bits this is −128 to +127.
- Example: −45. 45 = 0010 1101 → invert: 1101 0010 → add 1: 1101 0011 = 0xD3. Check: 0xD3 = 211 and 211 − 256 = −45.
- Overflow happens when two numbers of the same sign add to a result of the other sign. Example: 100 + 50 in 8 bits gives 1001 0110, which reads as −106. In hardware, overflow = carry into the MSB XOR carry out of the MSB.

Adder circuits
- Half adder: S = A ⊕ B, C = AB.
- Full adder (adds a carry-in too): S = A ⊕ B ⊕ Cin, Cout = AB + Cin(A ⊕ B).
- Ripple-carry adder: n full adders in a chain, each carry-out feeding the next carry-in. It is simple, but the worst-case delay grows in proportion to n because a carry may have to ripple through every stage.
- Subtraction: A − B = A + B' + 1. Put an XOR gate on each B input, controlled by a SUB line. SUB = 1 inverts B, and the same SUB line feeds the first carry-in to supply the +1. One circuit then adds or subtracts.

Exam tips: show the conversion steps explicitly, check two's complement answers by converting back, and be able to draw a full adder from gates and explain why a ripple-carry adder is slow for wide words.

Combinational versus sequential logic
- In combinational logic the outputs depend only on the present inputs.
- In sequential logic the outputs also depend on past inputs, because the circuit stores state. Memory, counters, registers and every processor rely on this.
- The basic storage element uses feedback: two gates cross-coupled so that each holds the other in place.

The SR latch
- Built from two cross-coupled NOR gates with inputs S (set) and R (reset).
- S = 1, R = 0 sets Q = 1. S = 0, R = 1 resets Q = 0. S = R = 0 holds the previous state.
- S = R = 1 is not allowed: both outputs go to 0 (so Q and Q' are no longer complements), and if both inputs then return to 0 together, the final state depends on which gate is faster.
- The NAND version has active-low inputs (S' and R'), and its forbidden input is both at 0.

Gated latches
- A clocked (gated) SR latch only responds to S and R while an enable or clock input is high.
- The D latch removes the forbidden state by feeding S = D and R = D'. While enabled, Q follows D (the latch is "transparent"). When the enable goes low, Q holds the last value.

Edge-triggered flip-flops
A transparent latch can let a change race through several stages in one clock pulse. A flip-flop samples its inputs only at a clock edge.
- D flip-flop: Q takes the value of D at the active clock edge, so Q⁺ = D. This is the building block of registers.
- JK flip-flop: J = K = 0 holds, J = 1 K = 0 sets, J = 0 K = 1 resets, and J = K = 1 toggles. Characteristic equation: Q⁺ = JQ' + K'Q.
- T (toggle) flip-flop: toggles when T = 1. It is a JK flip-flop with J = K = T.

Excitation table for the JK flip-flop
This is used in design: it tells you which J and K are needed for each transition.
- 0 → 0: J = 0, K = X.
- 0 → 1: J = 1, K = X.
- 1 → 0: J = X, K = 1.
- 1 → 1: J = X, K = 0.
The don't-cares are what make JK designs simplify well.

Practical points
- Setup time: D must be stable for a short time before the clock edge. Hold time: it must stay stable for a short time after. Violating these can leave the output unpredictable.
- Asynchronous preset and clear inputs force Q immediately, regardless of the clock. They are used for initialising a circuit at power-up.
- Timing diagrams for flip-flops should show outputs changing only just after the active edge, delayed by the propagation delay.

Exam tips: memorise the JK truth table, characteristic equation and excitation table, explain clearly the difference between a level-sensitive latch and an edge-triggered flip-flop, and explain why S = R = 1 is forbidden.

notes.h: Counters, shift registers and serial communication
notes.body:
Asynchronous (ripple) counters
- A chain of toggle flip-flops. The first is clocked by the system clock, and each later one is clocked by the output of the one before.
- Each stage divides the frequency by 2, so an n-stage chain counts from 0 to 2ⁿ − 1. It is also a simple frequency divider.
- Drawback: each stage waits for the one before, so delays add up. During a change such as 0111 → 1000 the outputs pass briefly through false intermediate values. Decoding these outputs can produce glitches, and the maximum clock rate falls as stages are added.
- A mod-N ripple counter can be made by detecting state N and resetting all stages. For a decade counter this means detecting 1010. The unwanted state appears briefly before the reset acts, which is a weakness of this method.

Synchronous counters
- All flip-flops share the same clock, so all outputs change together, one propagation delay after the edge.
- For a binary up-counter with JK or T flip-flops, a stage toggles when all lower bits are 1: T₀ = 1, T₁ = Q₀, T₂ = Q₀Q₁, T₃ = Q₀Q₁Q₂.
- Any sequence, not just binary, can be designed with the state-diagram method (next topic).

Shift registers
- A row of D flip-flops on a common clock, each D input fed from the previous Q. On each edge the data move one place.
- Types by input and output: serial-in serial-out (a delay line), serial-in parallel-out (serial-to-parallel conversion), parallel-in serial-out (parallel-to-serial), and parallel-in parallel-out (a storage register).
- Shifting a binary number one place left multiplies it by 2, and shifting right divides by 2 (for unsigned numbers).
- Feeding the last output back to the first input gives a ring counter.

Serial communication
Sending data one bit at a time needs fewer wires than sending a whole word at once. Shift registers do the conversion at each end.
- Asynchronous serial (as in a UART): the line idles at 1. Each character starts with a start bit (0), then the data bits, least significant first, an optional parity bit, then one or more stop bits (1). Transmitter and receiver agree the bit rate in advance. The receiver resynchronises on each start bit.
- Example: with 8 data bits, no parity and 1 stop bit, each byte takes 10 bit-times. At 9600 bit/s that is 960 bytes per second.
- Synchronous serial sends a clock line alongside the data, so no start and stop bits are needed.

Exam tips: be able to draw a 3- or 4-bit ripple counter and its timing diagram, explain why synchronous counters are preferred at high speed, and describe how a shift register converts between serial and parallel data.

A sequencer, or finite-state machine, is a sequential circuit that steps through defined states in response to a clock and inputs. The 1P3 objectives ask you to go all the way from a problem statement to a JK flip-flop circuit.

State diagrams
- Each state is a circle. Arrows show the transitions, labelled with the input condition that causes them.
- Moore machine: the outputs depend only on the current state, so they are written inside the circles.
- Mealy machine: the outputs depend on the state and the inputs, so they are written on the arrows.

The design procedure
1. Turn the problem statement into a state diagram. Decide what each state must "remember".
2. Write the state table: present state, input, next state, output.
3. Assign binary codes to the states. n flip-flops give up to 2ⁿ states.
4. For each flip-flop and each row, use the excitation table to find the J and K values needed.
5. Simplify each J, K and output function with a K-map, using unused states as don't-cares.
6. Check the unused states. Work out where each would go next, and make sure the machine cannot get stuck outside the intended sequence. If necessary, give unused states explicit next states.
7. Draw the circuit.

Worked example: mod-3 counter 00 → 01 → 10 → 00
States are written Q₁Q₀, and 11 is unused.
- Q₁: from 00 it stays 0, so J₁ = 0, K₁ = X. From 01 it goes 0 → 1, so J₁ = 1, K₁ = X. From 10 it goes 1 → 0, so J₁ = X, K₁ = 1. The row for 11 is all don't-cares.
- So J₁ = Q₀ and K₁ = 1.
- Q₀: from 00 it goes 0 → 1, so J₀ = 1. From 01 it goes 1 → 0, so K₀ = 1. From 10 it stays 0, so J₀ = 0.
- So J₀ = Q₁' and K₀ = 1.
- Check the sequence. From 00: J₁ = 0, K₁ = 1 gives Q₁ = 0, and J₀ = K₀ = 1 toggles Q₀ to 1, giving 01. From 01: J₁ = K₁ = 1 toggles Q₁ to 1, and Q₀ toggles to 0, giving 10. From 10: Q₁ resets to 0, and J₀ = 0, K₀ = 1 resets Q₀ to 0, giving 00.
- Check the unused state 11. J₁ = Q₀ = 1 and K₁ = 1 toggle Q₁ to 0. J₀ = Q₁' = 0 and K₀ = 1 reset Q₀ to 0. The machine goes to 00, so it is self-correcting.

Why unused states matter
At power-up, or after electrical noise, the flip-flops can land in any code. A good design always returns to the main sequence within a few clocks, or uses a reset to start in a known state.

Exam tips: lay out the state table and the excitation columns neatly, because most marks are for method. Always state what happens in unused states, and verify your final equations by stepping through the sequence.

A digital-to-analogue converter (DAC) turns an n-bit number D into a proportional voltage. Two classic resistor networks are in the syllabus.

Weighted-resistor DAC
- Each bit drives a resistor into the virtual earth of an inverting op-amp summing amplifier. The MSB uses R, the next 2R, then 4R, 8R and so on, so each bit's current is half that of the bit above.
- For 4 bits with logic-1 voltage Vref and feedback resistor Rf: Vout = −Vref(Rf/R)(b₃ + b₂/2 + b₁/4 + b₀/8).
- Example: R = 10 kΩ (so 20, 40, 80 kΩ for the lower bits), Rf = 5 kΩ, Vref = 5 V, input 1011. Then Vout = −5 × 0.5 × (1 + 0 + 0.25 + 0.125) = −3.4375 V. Check: 11/16 × 5 V = 3.4375 V.
- Problem: an n-bit converter needs resistors spanning a ratio of 2ⁿ⁻¹, all accurate to better than the LSB weight. That is impractical for more than a few bits.

R-2R ladder DAC
- It uses only two resistor values, R and 2R, which are easy to match accurately.
- In the common voltage arrangement, each bit switches its 2R leg between 0 V and Vref. Series resistors R join the nodes, and the LSB end is terminated with 2R to ground.
- Reduce the circuit by Thévenin's theorem one node at a time. Each node looks like a source of resistance R, and each step halves the contribution of the bits already included. The output is Vout = Vref·D/2ⁿ, with output resistance R, so it is usually buffered by an op-amp.
- Resolution: one LSB = Vref/2ⁿ. For 8 bits and Vref = 5 V this is about 19.5 mV, and full scale is 5 × 255/256 ≈ 4.98 V. The input 1000 0000 (D = 128) gives exactly 2.5 V.

Schmitt-trigger inputs
- A normal gate has one switching threshold. A slowly changing or noisy input that hovers near it can make the output chatter between 0 and 1 many times.
- A Schmitt trigger has hysteresis: two thresholds. The output switches high only when the input rises above the upper threshold VT+, and switches low only when it falls below the lower threshold VT−.
- Noise smaller than the hysteresis gap (VT+ − VT−) cannot cause false switching. Slow edges are turned into clean, fast ones.
- Uses: switch and push-button inputs, signals arriving over long cables, and squaring up sine waves.
- An op-amp version uses positive feedback. For an inverting Schmitt trigger with a divider of R₁ (from the + input to ground) and R₂ (from the output to the + input), the thresholds are ±Vsat·R₁/(R₁ + R₂).
- Draw the transfer characteristic as a loop, with arrows showing the direction of travel.

Exam tips: be able to derive the weighted-resistor output from the summing amplifier, explain why the R-2R ladder is preferred, work out the LSB step for a given number of bits, and sketch a Schmitt-trigger hysteresis loop.

notes.h: Microprocessor architecture, memory and address decoding
notes.body:
A simple microprocessor system
- CPU: the arithmetic logic unit (ALU), registers, the program counter (PC, holding the address of the next instruction), the instruction register and a control unit.
- Memory: ROM or flash for the program, and RAM for changing data.
- Input/output: ports, timers, converters.
- Buses connect them. The address bus is driven by the CPU and says which location is wanted. The data bus is bidirectional and carries the value. The control bus carries signals such as read/write, chip select and the clock.
- The CPU repeats a fetch–decode–execute cycle: fetch the instruction at PC, increment PC, decode it, then execute it, possibly reading or writing memory.
- In a von Neumann machine program and data share one memory. In a Harvard machine, such as the PIC, they are separate, so an instruction fetch and a data access can overlap and the two memories can have different word widths.

Memory devices
- ROM is non-volatile. Its variants include mask ROM, PROM, EPROM (erased by UV light), EEPROM and flash (both erased electrically).
- RAM is volatile. Static RAM stores each bit in a flip-flop: it is fast and needs no refresh. Dynamic RAM stores bits as charge on capacitors: it is denser but must be refreshed.
- Pins: n address lines select 2ⁿ locations, and the data lines set the word width. An 8K × 8 RAM therefore has 13 address lines (2¹³ = 8192) and 8 data lines.
- Control pins are usually active-low: CS' (chip select), OE' (output enable, for reading) and WE' (write enable).

Tri-state outputs and buses
- A tri-state output can be 0, 1 or high-impedance (effectively disconnected).
- Many devices can share one data bus as long as only the selected device drives it. The others float.
- If two devices drive opposite values at once (bus contention), large currents can flow, which corrupts data and can cause damage. Address decoding prevents this.

Address decoding
The decoder looks at the upper address lines and enables exactly one device.
- Example with a 16-bit address bus (64K locations). Place a 32K ROM at 0000–7FFF. It is selected when A15 = 0 and uses A14–A0 internally.
- Place an 8K RAM at 8000–9FFF. In binary 8000 = 1000 0000 0000 0000 and 9FFF = 1001 1111 1111 1111, so A15 = 1, A14 = 0, A13 = 0 throughout, and A12–A0 address inside the chip. Its select is CS' = (A15·A14'·A13')'.
- Full decoding uses every upper address line, so each device appears exactly once in the memory map.
- Partial decoding ignores some lines to save logic. If the RAM above were selected by A15 = 1 alone, it would respond across 8000–FFFF and appear four times (aliases), and nothing else could be put there.

Exam tips: draw a memory map with hex boundaries and convert them to binary to see which address lines are fixed. Count address lines from the device size, and explain why tri-state outputs are needed on a shared bus.

notes.h: PIC programming and the PIC12F629/675 instruction set
notes.body:
The course's programming examples use the Microchip PIC12F629/675, an 8-pin microcontroller (CPU, memory and I/O on one chip).

The device (from the data sheet)
- Harvard architecture with 14-bit instruction words, 1024 words of flash program memory, 64 bytes of RAM and 128 bytes of EEPROM.
- 35 instructions; all are single-cycle except branches, which take two cycles.
- An 8-level hardware stack holds return addresses.
- Six I/O pins, GP0–GP5, of which GP3 is input only. The 675 adds a 10-bit ADC with 4 channels; the 629 has no ADC.
- An instruction cycle is four oscillator periods: 1 µs with the 4 MHz internal oscillator.

Registers
- W, the working register, is the accumulator. Most operations combine W with a file register f.
- Special function registers include STATUS (flags Z, zero, bit 2; DC, digit carry, bit 1; C, carry, bit 0; and RP0, bank select, bit 5), GPIO (the pin values) and TRISIO (pin direction: 1 = input, 0 = output, located in bank 1).
- The remaining file registers are general-purpose RAM for your variables.

Instruction types
- Byte-oriented, for example ADDWF f,d or MOVF f,d. The bit d chooses the destination: W (d = 0) or back into f (d = 1).
- Bit-oriented: BSF f,b and BCF f,b set and clear a bit. BTFSS and BTFSC test a bit and skip the next instruction if it is set or clear. This, followed by a GOTO, is the PIC's conditional branch.
- Literal and control: MOVLW k, ADDLW k, ANDLW k, GOTO, CALL, RETURN, RETLW k.
- On a subtraction, C = 1 means there was no borrow.

Addressing modes
- Immediate (literal): the operand is in the instruction, as in MOVLW 0x3F.
- Direct: the instruction contains the register address, as in MOVWF 0x20.
- Indirect: put an address in FSR and access it through INDF. This is useful for stepping through a table.

Example: make GP0 an output and toggle it
    BSF   STATUS,RP0   ; bank 1
    BCF   TRISIO,0     ; GP0 output
    BCF   STATUS,RP0   ; back to bank 0
LOOP MOVLW 0x01
    XORWF GPIO,F       ; flip bit 0
    CALL  DELAY
    GOTO  LOOP
(At reset GP0 and GP1 are assigned to the comparator, so write 0x07 to CMCON to make them digital on either device; on the 675 also clear ANSEL to turn off the ADC inputs.)

Timing a delay loop
MOVLW N, MOVWF C, then LOOP: DECFSZ C,F; GOTO LOOP takes 2 + 3(N − 1) + 2 = 3N + 1 cycles. N = 250 gives 751 µs at 4 MHz. Nest two loops for longer delays.

Stack, subroutines and reset
- CALL pushes the return address and jumps. RETURN or RETLW pops it. There are only 8 levels and no overflow warning, so do not nest too deeply.
- On reset the program counter starts at address 0x000. The interrupt vector is 0x004.

Assembly and higher-level languages
- The assembler translates each mnemonic into one 14-bit machine-code word.
- A compiler translates a language such as C into many instructions. It is quicker to write and easier to port, but gives less direct control over timing and code size.

Exam tips: be able to explain the fetch–execute operation of the PIC, write short routines with conditional branches, and count the cycles a routine takes.

cards.b: NAND and NOR: any Boolean function can be built from NAND gates alone, or from NOR gates alone.
NMH = VOH(min) − VIH(min): how much noise a high output can tolerate before the next input might misread it.
VOH(min) 2.4 V, VIH(min) 2.0 V, VIL(max) 0.8 V, VOL(max) 0.4 V, so NMH = NML = 0.4 V.
Two PMOS transistors in parallel from the supply to the output, two NMOS in series from the output to ground.

cards.f: Why CMOS has low static power
cards.b: In either steady state one of the pull-up and pull-down networks is off, so no DC path from supply to ground. Power is mainly dynamic, about C·V²·f.
When the output is low the pull-down transistor conducts through the load, so current flows continuously from the supply.
Time between the input and output crossing 50% of the swing: tPHL for a falling output, tPLH for a rising one.
(A + B)' = A'·B' and (AB)' = A' + B'.
A + AB = A, and A + A'B = A + B.
Rows and columns in Gray-code order (00, 01, 11, 10) so neighbouring cells differ in one variable; the map wraps round.
Groups of 1, 2, 4, 8 cells; as large as possible, as few as possible; overlaps and wrap-round allowed; a group of 2ᵏ removes k variables.
Input combinations that never occur or whose output doesn't matter: use them as 1s if they enlarge a group, otherwise ignore them.

cards.f: Majority function of A, B, C
cards.b: M = AB + BC + AC (1 when at least two inputs are 1).
Replace both layers of a two-level AND–OR circuit by NAND gates: NAND–NAND equals AND–OR by De Morgan.
The output should stay at 1 during an input change but briefly drops to 0 because of unequal path delays.

cards.f: Spotting a hazard on a K-map
cards.b: Two adjacent 1-cells covered by different, non-overlapping groups: the transition between them can glitch.
Add the redundant consensus group covering the adjacent cells, e.g. F = AC' + BC becomes AC' + BC + AB.
Entity: the interface (ports in and out). Architecture: the behaviour or structure inside.
Concurrent: all assignments act simultaneously like wired gates, not one after another like program statements.
Inside a process: if rising_edge(clk) then q <= d; end if;
−2ⁿ⁻¹ to 2ⁿ⁻¹ − 1; for 8 bits, −128 to +127.
Invert every bit and add 1. E.g. 45 = 0010 1101 → −45 = 1101 0011 (0xD3).
Each decimal digit coded in 4 bits: 183 = 0001 1000 0011. Codes 1010–1111 unused.
Successive values differ in only one bit; binary to Gray: g = b XOR (b >> 1).
S = A ⊕ B ⊕ Cin; Cout = AB + Cin(A ⊕ B).
Overflow if two same-sign operands give a result of the other sign; in hardware, carry into MSB XOR carry out of MSB.
XOR each B bit with SUB and feed SUB into the carry-in: SUB = 1 gives A + B' + 1 = A − B.
Combinational outputs depend only on present inputs; sequential outputs also depend on stored state (past inputs).
S = R = 1: both outputs go to 0, and releasing both together leaves an unpredictable state.
Latch is transparent while enabled (Q follows D); flip-flop samples D only at the active clock edge.
00 hold, 10 set, 01 reset, 11 toggle.
Q⁺ = JQ' + K'Q.
D must be stable for the setup time before the clock edge and for the hold time after it.
Stage delays add up, so outputs pass through false intermediate states and the maximum clock rate falls with more stages.
T₀ = 1, T₁ = Q₀, T₂ = Q₀Q₁, T₃ = Q₀Q₁Q₂: a stage toggles when all lower bits are 1.
Counts 0 to 2ⁿ − 1; each stage divides the clock frequency by 2.
Data enter one bit per clock and are read out together: a serial-to-parallel converter.
Line idles at 1; start bit 0; data bits LSB first; optional parity; stop bit(s) 1.
10 bit-times per byte (start + 8 data + stop), so 960 bytes per second.
Moore: outputs depend only on the state. Mealy: outputs depend on state and inputs.
State diagram → state table → state assignment → excitation table → K-maps for J, K → check unused states → circuit.
At power-up or after noise the circuit may land in one; it must return to the main sequence and not lock up.
J₁ = Q₀, K₁ = 1, J₀ = Q₁', K₀ = 1; unused 11 goes to 00 (self-correcting).

cards.f: Number of flip-flops for S states
cards.b: The smallest n with 2ⁿ ≥ S; e.g. 5 states need 3 flip-flops.
Lists present state, input, next state and output for every combination: the bridge from diagram to logic.
Vout = −Vref(Rf/R)(b₃ + b₂/2 + b₁/4 + b₀/8), with resistors R, 2R, 4R, 8R from MSB to LSB.
It needs resistors spanning a 2ⁿ⁻¹ ratio, all precise to better than one LSB: impractical for many bits.
Vout = Vref·D/2ⁿ with output resistance R; only two resistor values are needed.
One LSB = Vref/2ⁿ; 8 bits with 5 V gives about 19.5 mV.
Gate with hysteresis: switches high above VT+ and low below VT−, rejecting noise smaller than the gap.
±Vsat·R₁/(R₁ + R₂), where R₂ feeds back from the output to the + input and R₁ goes from + to ground.
Address: from the CPU, selects a location. Data: bidirectional, carries values. Control: R/W, chip select, clock.
Harvard has separate program and data memories (as in the PIC); von Neumann shares one memory for both.
13 address lines (2¹³ = 8192) and 8 data lines.
Can be 0, 1 or high-impedance, so many devices can share a bus with only the selected one driving it.
SRAM: flip-flop per bit, fast, no refresh. DRAM: charge on a capacitor, denser, needs refreshing.
Ignoring some address lines: simpler logic, but each device appears at several aliased addresses.
1024 words of 14-bit flash program memory, 64 bytes RAM, 128 bytes EEPROM.
Bit test f, skip the next instruction if bit b is set. Used with GOTO to make conditional branches.
Load the target address into FSR and read or write INDF.
C (bit 0), DC (bit 1), Z (bit 2); RP0 (bit 5) selects bank 1.
Reset: program counter starts at 0x000. Interrupt vector: 0x004.
8 levels; deeper nesting of CALLs overwrites return addresses without warning.
C = 1 means no borrow (result ≥ 0); C = 0 means a borrow occurred.

questions.q: A logic family has VOH(min) = 4.4 V, VOL(max) = 0.1 V, VIH(min) = 3.5 V and VIL(max) = 1.5 V. What are the high and low noise margins?
questions.why: NMH = VOH(min) − VIH(min) = 4.4 − 3.5 = 0.9 V and NML = VIL(max) − VOL(max) = 1.5 − 0.1 = 1.4 V. NMH = 1.4 V, NML = 0.9 V swaps the two margins; NML = 0.1 V just uses VOL(max) on its own; 2.9 V and 3.4 V come from subtracting mismatched pairs (VOH − VIL and VIH − VOL).

questions.q: In a CMOS two-input NOR gate, how are the transistors arranged?
options: PMOS in series to the supply, NMOS in parallel to ground
PMOS in parallel to the supply, NMOS in series to ground
PMOS and NMOS both in series
A single NMOS with a resistor load
questions.why: NOR must pull high only when both inputs are 0, so the PMOS (on when their input is low) are in series; it pulls low if either input is 1, so the NMOS are in parallel. Parallel PMOS / series NMOS is the NAND; all-series would not give complementary networks; a resistor load is NMOS logic, not CMOS.

questions.q: Explain why a CMOS inverter dissipates very little power when its input is steady, and why its power consumption rises with clock frequency.
markScheme: Describes the inverter: PMOS to supply, NMOS to ground, gates joined
In each steady state one transistor is off, so there is no DC path from supply to ground
On each transition the load capacitance is charged/discharged (and both devices briefly conduct)
Dynamic power about C·V²·f, so it is proportional to switching frequency
questions.modelAnswer: A CMOS inverter is a PMOS transistor from the supply to the output and an NMOS from the output to ground, with both gates driven by the input. With the input high the NMOS is on and the PMOS off, so the output is held low; with the input low the reverse holds. In either steady state one transistor is off, so there is no conducting path from supply to ground and only tiny leakage current flows. Power is used when the output switches: the load capacitance C must be charged through the PMOS and discharged through the NMOS, and during the transition both devices briefly conduct. The energy per cycle is of order C·V², so average power is roughly C·V²·f and rises in proportion to the switching frequency (and with the square of the supply voltage).

questions.q: Which expression is the minimal sum of products for F(A,B,C,D) = Σm(0, 2, 8, 10)?
questions.why: The four minterms are the corners of the K-map (B = 0 and D = 0 with A and C free), which wrap round into one group of four: B'D'. A'B'D' covers only 0 and 2; the two-term answer is correct but not minimal; BD covers 5, 7, 13, 15.

questions.q: Using De Morgan's theorem, (A'B + C)' equals:
questions.why: (A'B + C)' = (A'B)'·C' = (A + B')·C'. The other options misapply the rule: either not changing the operator or not complementing every literal.

questions.q: A car's warning buzzer B must sound when the ignition is on (I = 1) and either the driver's seat belt is unfastened (S = 0) or a door is open (D = 1). It must also sound whenever the headlights are on (L = 1) and the ignition is off. Write a Boolean expression for B, simplify it, and state how you would implement it using only NAND gates.
markScheme: B = I(S' + D) + LI'
Expands to IS' + ID + I'L, which is already a minimal SOP (check on a K-map)
Correct use of inversion for S' and I' (NAND with inputs tied)
Two-level NAND–NAND: one NAND per product term, then a NAND of their outputs
Clear statement that NAND–NAND realises AND–OR by De Morgan
questions.modelAnswer: From the words: B = I(S' + D) + L·I'. Expanding gives B = IS' + ID + I'L. On a four-variable K-map the three terms are distinct prime implicants and none can be dropped, so this is minimal. For NAND-only logic, first make S' and I' with NAND gates whose inputs are tied together. Then each product term is a two-input NAND: (I·S')', (I·D)', (I'·L)'. A three-input NAND of these three outputs gives ((IS')'·(ID)'·(I'L)')' = IS' + ID + I'L by De Morgan. So the circuit is a two-level NAND–NAND network plus two NAND inverters.

questions.q: F = AC' + BC. For which input change is a static-1 hazard possible?
questions.why: With A = B = 1, F = C' + C = 1, but the C and C' paths have different delays, so a change in C can let both terms be 0 briefly. In the other cases a single term controls the output (or the output genuinely changes), so there is no 1 → 0 → 1 glitch from unequal path delays.

questions.q: In VHDL, what does the entity declaration describe?
options: The ports (inputs and outputs) of the design
The clock frequency of the target device
The order in which statements are executed
questions.why: The entity is the external interface: the names, directions and types of the ports. The architecture holds the logic; VHDL does not set clock frequency in the entity; and concurrent statements have no execution order.

questions.q: Using a timing diagram, explain how the circuit F = AC' + BC can glitch when A = B = 1 and C falls from 1 to 0, and show how to remove the hazard.
markScheme: States that F should stay at 1 since F = C' + C
Timing: BC falls immediately when C falls; C' (and AC') rises only after the inverter delay
Shows a gap where both product terms are 0 so F briefly drops: static-1 hazard
K-map: the two groups are adjacent but do not overlap
Add consensus term AB: F = AC' + BC + AB keeps F = 1 throughout
questions.modelAnswer: With A = B = 1, F = C' + C, which should be constantly 1. Draw C falling at time t₀. The term BC falls one AND-gate delay after t₀. The inverter output C' only rises one inverter delay after t₀, and AC' rises one AND delay later still. So there is an interval where both AND outputs are 0, and F (after the OR delay) dips to 0 before returning to 1: a static-1 hazard. On the K-map, AC' and BC are adjacent groups that do not overlap, and the cells ABC' and ABC (which differ only in C) are covered by different groups. Adding the consensus group AB, which covers both cells, gives F = AC' + BC + AB. This is logically identical but AB = 1 holds F high regardless of the C transition, so the glitch disappears.

questions.q: What is the 8-bit two's complement representation of −20?
Two 8-bit two's complement numbers 0111 0000 (+112) and 0010 0000 (+32) are added. What happens?
options: The result 1001 0000 reads as −112, so overflow has occurred
The result is +144 with no overflow
The result is 0001 0000 with a carry out
The adder produces 0 and sets the zero flag
questions.why: 112 + 32 = 144 exceeds +127. The sum bits are 1001 0000, which in two's complement is 144 − 256 = −112: two positive operands gave a negative result, which signals overflow. 8-bit signed numbers cannot represent +144; there is no carry out of the MSB here; the result is not zero.

questions.q: Draw (describe) a full adder using XOR, AND and OR gates and write its equations. Explain how n full adders and n XOR gates can make an n-bit adder/subtractor, and why the delay grows with n.
markScheme: S = A ⊕ B ⊕ Cin
Cout = AB + Cin(A ⊕ B), using two XOR, two AND, one OR
Ripple chain: carry-out of each stage to carry-in of the next
Subtraction via A + B' + 1: XOR each B with SUB, SUB into first carry-in
Worst-case carry must ripple through all n stages, so delay ∝ n
questions.modelAnswer: A full adder adds A, B and a carry-in. A first XOR gives P = A ⊕ B; a second XOR gives S = P ⊕ Cin. Two AND gates form AB and Cin·P, and an OR gives Cout = AB + Cin(A ⊕ B). For an n-bit adder, chain n full adders so each carry-out drives the next stage's carry-in (ripple carry). To subtract, use A − B = A + B' + 1 in two's complement: place an XOR gate on each B input with its other input tied to a control line SUB. When SUB = 1 the B bits are inverted, and SUB is also fed into the first carry-in to add the 1; when SUB = 0 the circuit adds. The worst case, such as adding 1 to 0111...1, needs a carry generated in the lowest stage to pass through every stage before the top sum bit settles, so the delay is proportional to n.

questions.q: A JK flip-flop has Q = 1. J = 1 and K = 1 at the next active clock edge. What is Q after the edge?
options: It depends on the previous value of J
questions.why: J = K = 1 is the toggle condition, so Q goes from 1 to 0. Q⁺ = JQ' + K'Q = 1·0 + 0·1 = 0. Unlike the SR latch, the JK has no forbidden input.

questions.q: Which statement about a D latch and a D flip-flop is correct?
options: The latch output follows D while it is enabled; the flip-flop changes only at the clock edge
Both change only at the rising clock edge
The flip-flop is transparent while the clock is high
The latch has a forbidden input combination
questions.why: A D latch is level-sensitive (transparent while enabled), whereas a D flip-flop is edge-triggered. The flip-flop is not transparent; the D latch removes the SR forbidden state by construction.

questions.q: Explain the operation of an SR latch made from two cross-coupled NOR gates, including why S = R = 1 is not allowed.
markScheme: Q = (R + Q')' and Q' = (S + Q)': cross-coupled feedback stores a bit
S = 1, R = 0 sets Q = 1; S = 0, R = 1 resets Q = 0
S = R = 0 holds the previous state
S = R = 1 forces both outputs to 0 (not complementary); returning both to 0 together gives an unpredictable state (race)
questions.modelAnswer: Each NOR gate's output feeds one input of the other: Q = (R + Q')' and Q' = (S + Q)'. If S = 1 and R = 0, Q' is forced to 0, so Q = (0 + 0)' = 1: the latch is set. If R = 1 and S = 0, Q is forced to 0 and Q' becomes 1: reset. With S = R = 0 each gate simply inverts the other's output, so whichever state existed is held: this is the memory. If S = R = 1, both NOR outputs are 0, so Q and Q' are no longer complements. Worse, if both inputs then return to 0 at the same time, both gates try to go to 1 and the final state depends on which is faster: a race. So the input S = R = 1 is forbidden.

questions.q: How many flip-flops does a ripple counter need to divide a 1 MHz clock down to 62.5 kHz?
questions.why: Each stage divides by 2; 1 MHz / 62.5 kHz = 16 = 2⁴, so 4 stages. 3 stages give 125 kHz; 5 give 31.25 kHz; 16 confuses the division ratio with the number of stages.

questions.q: A UART sends characters with 1 start bit, 8 data bits, no parity and 2 stop bits at 4800 bit/s. What is the maximum character rate?
questions.why: Each character takes 1 + 8 + 2 = 11 bit-times, so 4800/11 ≈ 436 per second. 480 assumes 10 bits; 600 assumes 8 bits with no framing; 4800 confuses bits with characters.

questions.q: Compare asynchronous (ripple) and synchronous binary counters, explaining why the synchronous design is preferred at high clock rates. Give the toggle conditions for a 3-bit synchronous up-counter.
markScheme: Ripple: each flip-flop clocked by previous output; only first by system clock
Ripple delays accumulate; outputs pass through false intermediate states; max clock rate falls with more stages
Synchronous: all flip-flops on common clock; outputs change together after one delay
Toggle conditions T₀ = 1, T₁ = Q₀, T₂ = Q₀Q₁
Synchronous needs extra gating logic but is faster and glitch-free to decode
questions.modelAnswer: In a ripple counter only the first toggle flip-flop is driven by the clock; each later stage is clocked by the output of the one before. It needs no extra logic, but every stage adds a propagation delay, so after an edge the outputs settle one after another. During a change such as 011 → 100 the counter briefly shows false states (010, 000) which can cause glitches if decoded, and the total settling time limits the clock rate as stages are added. In a synchronous counter all flip-flops share the clock and change together, one flip-flop delay after the edge, with combinational logic deciding which ones toggle. For a 3-bit up-counter using T (or JK with J = K) flip-flops: T₀ = 1, T₁ = Q₀ and T₂ = Q₀Q₁, since a bit toggles when all lower bits are 1. The extra AND gates cost a little, but the counter is faster and its outputs can be decoded safely.

questions.q: A synchronous sequencer must step through 6 distinct states. What is the minimum number of flip-flops, and how many unused codes remain?
questions.why: You need 2ⁿ ≥ 6, so n = 3 giving 8 codes, of which 2 are unused and must be checked so the machine cannot lock up. 2 flip-flops give only 4 codes; 6 flip-flops (one-hot) would work but is not the minimum; 3 flip-flops do leave 2 spare codes.

questions.q: For a JK flip-flop that must go from Q = 1 to Q = 1 on the next clock, which inputs are required?
questions.why: To stay at 1 the flip-flop must not reset or toggle, so K = 0; J can be either value, because with K = 0 both J = 1 (set) and J = 0 (hold) leave Q = 1. J = 1, K = X is 0 → 1; J = 0, K = X is 0 → 0; J = X, K = 1 is 1 → 0.

questions.q: Design a synchronous counter using two JK flip-flops (Q₁Q₀) that counts 00 → 01 → 10 → 00. Derive J and K for each flip-flop and check what happens if the counter starts in state 11.
markScheme: State table with next states 01, 10, 00 and 11 as don't-care
Excitation entries correctly derived for each transition
J₁ = Q₀, K₁ = 1
J₀ = Q₁', K₀ = 1
Verification of the main sequence
Unused state 11 goes to 00: self-correcting
questions.modelAnswer: State table (Q₁Q₀ → next): 00 → 01, 01 → 10, 10 → 00, 11 → X. Flip-flop 1: 00 → Q₁ stays 0 (J₁ = 0, K₁ = X); 01 → Q₁ goes 0 → 1 (J₁ = 1, K₁ = X); 10 → Q₁ goes 1 → 0 (J₁ = X, K₁ = 1). Using don't-cares, J₁ = Q₀ and K₁ = 1. Flip-flop 0: 00 → Q₀ goes 0 → 1 (J₀ = 1, K₀ = X); 01 → 1 → 0 (J₀ = X, K₀ = 1); 10 → stays 0 (J₀ = 0, K₀ = X). So J₀ = Q₁' and K₀ = 1. Check: from 00, Q₁ reset (stays 0) and Q₀ toggles to 1 → 01; from 01, both toggle → 10; from 10, Q₁ resets to 0 and Q₀ is reset (J₀ = 0, K₀ = 1) → 00. From 11: J₁ = 1, K₁ = 1 toggles Q₁ to 0; J₀ = 0, K₀ = 1 resets Q₀ to 0; so 11 → 00, and the counter is self-correcting.

questions.q: An 8-bit R-2R ladder DAC with Vref = 5 V receives the input 0100 0000. What is its (unloaded) output voltage?
questions.why: Vout = Vref·D/2ⁿ = 5 × 64/256 = 1.25 V. 2.5 V is the output for 1000 0000; 0.625 V is for 0010 0000; 1.25 mV confuses volts and millivolts.

questions.q: What is the main purpose of a Schmitt-trigger input on a digital gate?
options: To provide hysteresis so slow or noisy inputs switch cleanly once
To increase the fan-out of the gate
To convert the input from analogue to binary code with n bits
To reduce the propagation delay of the gate
questions.why: Two thresholds (VT+ above VT−) mean noise smaller than the hysteresis gap cannot cause repeated switching, and slow edges become fast ones. It does not change fan-out, is not a multi-bit ADC and does not reduce delay.

questions.q: A 4-bit weighted-resistor DAC uses an inverting summing amplifier with Rf = 5 kΩ and input resistors 10, 20, 40 and 80 kΩ (MSB to LSB). Logic 1 is 5 V. Find the output for input 1011 and for full scale, and explain why this design is rarely used for 12-bit converters.
markScheme: Vout = −Rf Σ(Vᵢ/Rᵢ)
12 bits needs resistor ratio 2¹¹ = 2048, all with tolerance better than one LSB
R-2R ladder preferred: only two values, easily matched
questions.modelAnswer: The summing amplifier gives Vout = −Rf(V₃/R₃ + V₂/R₂ + V₁/R₁ + V₀/R₀). For 1011 the bits at 1 are the MSB (10 kΩ), bit 1 (40 kΩ) and the LSB (80 kΩ): currents 0.5 mA, 0.125 mA and 0.0625 mA, total 0.6875 mA, so Vout = −5 kΩ × 0.6875 mA = −3.4375 V (= −(11/16) × 5 V). For full scale 1111 the total current is 0.5 + 0.25 + 0.125 + 0.0625 = 0.9375 mA, so Vout = −4.6875 V. A 12-bit version would need resistors spanning a ratio of 2¹¹ = 2048 (e.g. 10 kΩ to 20.48 MΩ), each accurate to much better than 1 part in 4096 of the MSB weight; such a spread of precise, temperature-matched resistors is impractical. The R-2R ladder needs only two values, which can be made and matched accurately, so it is used instead.

questions.q: A memory chip has 15 address lines and 8 data lines. What is its capacity?
questions.why: 2¹⁵ = 32 768 locations, each 8 bits wide. 15K confuses lines with kilobytes; 16K would need 14 lines; the data width is 8, not 15.

questions.q: On a 16-bit address bus an 8K RAM is selected only by the condition A15 = 1, A14 = 1, A13 = 0. What range does it occupy?
questions.why: A15 A14 A13 = 110 gives the top hex digit 1100 or 1101 (C or D), with A12–A0 free: C000–DFFF. 100 gives 8000–9FFF; 111 gives E000–FFFF; 101 gives A000–BFFF.

questions.q: Explain the purpose of tri-state outputs in a microprocessor system and describe how address decoding ensures correct operation of a shared data bus. Distinguish full and partial decoding.
markScheme: Tri-state: 0, 1 or high impedance; lets many devices connect to one bus
Only the selected device may drive the bus; others float
Contention if two drive at once: corruption, excess current, possible damage
Decoder uses upper address lines (and control signals) to assert exactly one chip select
Full decoding uses all upper lines (unique addresses); partial ignores some (simpler, but aliases and wasted address space)
questions.modelAnswer: Memory and I/O devices all connect to the same data bus. A tri-state output can drive 0 or 1, or go to a high-impedance state in which it is effectively disconnected. When a device's chip select (and output enable) is inactive, its outputs are high-impedance, so only the selected device drives the bus. If two devices drove opposite values at once (bus contention) the data would be corrupted and large currents could flow. The address decoder prevents this: it examines the upper address lines, together with control signals such as read/write, and asserts exactly one chip-select line for each address. In full decoding every upper address line is used, so each device occupies a unique range. In partial decoding some lines are ignored, which simplifies the logic but makes devices appear at several aliased addresses and wastes address space.

questions.q: After MOVLW 0x05 then ADDWF COUNT,W, where COUNT contains 0x0A, which is true?
questions.why: ADDWF f,d adds W to f; with d = W the result goes to W, leaving COUNT = 0x0A. 0x05 + 0x0A = 0x0F. Writing to COUNT would need d = F; the result is not stored in both; 0x50 is not the sum.

questions.q: Which instruction pair makes the PIC execute GOTO HIGH only when bit 3 of GPIO is 1?
questions.why: BTFSC skips the next instruction if the bit is clear, so GOTO HIGH runs only when the bit is 1. BTFSS skips when the bit is set, giving the opposite; BSF and BCF change the bit rather than test it.

questions.q: Write a short PIC12F629/675 assembly routine that sets GP0 as an output and then repeatedly copies the state of input GP3 to GP0. Explain the role of each instruction and state how long one pass of your main loop takes at 4 MHz.
markScheme: Bank switch with BSF STATUS,RP0, clear TRISIO bit 0, return with BCF STATUS,RP0
Test GP3 with BTFSS/BTFSC
Set or clear GP0 with BSF/BCF accordingly
Loop with GOTO
Correct cycle count with skips and GOTOs taking 2 cycles; 1 µs per cycle
questions.modelAnswer:
One routine:
    BSF STATUS,RP0   ; select bank 1
    BCF TRISIO,0     ; GP0 output (GP3 is input only)
    BCF STATUS,RP0   ; back to bank 0
LOOP BTFSS GPIO,3     ; skip next if GP3 = 1
    GOTO LOW
    BSF GPIO,0       ; GP3 = 1: drive GP0 high
    GOTO LOOP
LOW  BCF GPIO,0       ; GP3 = 0: drive GP0 low
    GOTO LOOP
(In practice, also write 0x07 to CMCON so GP0 is a digital pin, clear ANSEL on the 675, and disable the MCLR function in the configuration word so GP3 works as an input.) Timing: if GP3 = 1, BTFSS skips (2 cycles), BSF (1), GOTO LOOP (2) = 5 cycles. If GP3 = 0, BTFSS does not skip (1), GOTO LOW (2), BCF (1), GOTO LOOP (2) = 6 cycles. At 4 MHz each cycle is 1 µs, so a pass takes 5 or 6 µs.

questions.q:
A circuit receives a BCD digit on inputs A, B, C, D (A is the most significant bit). Its output F must be 1 when the digit is divisible by 3 (0, 3, 6 or 9) and 0 for other valid digits.
(a) Write F as a sum of minterms and identify the don't-care terms. [3]
(b) Use a Karnaugh map to find a minimal sum-of-products expression for F. [8]
(c) Show how F could be implemented using only NAND gates (inverters may be made from NAND gates). [4]
(d) Explain what a static hazard is and whether your circuit from (b) can exhibit one when the input changes from 3 to 11 (binary 0011 to 1011). [5]
markScheme: (a) F = Σm(0, 3, 6, 9) with don't cares d(10, 11, 12, 13, 14, 15) since codes 1010–1111 never occur in BCD
(b) Correct Gray-ordered K-map with 1s, 0s and Xs
(b) Groups: 9 with 11, 13, 15 → AD; 3 with 11 → B'CD; 6 with 14 → BCD'; 0 alone → A'B'C'D'
(b) F = A'B'C'D' + B'CD + BCD' + AD, with justification that no larger groups exist
(c) First-level NANDs for each product term, inverted inputs via NAND inverters
(c) Second-level 4-input NAND gives the OR by De Morgan
(d) Definition: momentary wrong output during a single input change due to unequal path delays
(d) 0011 and 1011 are both covered by B'CD, so F stays 1 with no hazard for this transition
questions.modelAnswer:
(a) Valid BCD digits are 0–9. F = 1 for 0 (0000), 3 (0011), 6 (0110) and 9 (1001), so F = Σm(0, 3, 6, 9). The codes 10–15 (1010 to 1111) never occur, so they are don't-cares: d(10, 11, 12, 13, 14, 15).

(b) Draw a four-variable K-map with AB labelling rows and CD labelling columns, both in the order 00, 01, 11, 10. Enter 1 at cells 0, 3, 6, 9, X at 10–15, and 0 elsewhere.
- Cell 9 (1001): its neighbours 11 (1011), 13 (1101) and 15 (1111) are don't-cares, so the four cells 9, 11, 13, 15 form a group where A = 1 and D = 1: AD.
- Cell 3 (0011): neighbours 1, 2 and 7 are 0, but 11 is a don't-care, so the pair {3, 11} gives B'CD. No group of four is possible: {3, 7, 11, 15} contains 7 = 0, {2, 3, 10, 11} contains 2 = 0, and {1, 3, 9, 11} contains 1 = 0.
- Cell 6 (0110): neighbours 2, 4 and 7 are 0, while 14 is a don't-care, so {6, 14} gives BCD'. Again no quad works, as each candidate contains a 0 (cells 4, 7 or 2).
- Cell 0 (0000): its neighbours 1, 2, 4 and 8 are all valid digits with F = 0, so it stands alone: A'B'C'D'.
Hence F = A'B'C'D' + B'CD + BCD' + AD. Check: digit 9 gives AD = 1; digit 5 (0101) gives 0 for every term; digit 8 (1000) has D = 0 and C = 0, so every term is 0.

(c) Make A', B', C', D' using NAND gates with their inputs tied together. Then form each product with a NAND: X₁ = (A'B'C'D')' with a 4-input NAND, X₂ = (B'CD)' and X₃ = (BCD')' with 3-input NANDs, and X₄ = (AD)' with a 2-input NAND. Finally F = (X₁X₂X₃X₄)', a 4-input NAND. By De Morgan this equals A'B'C'D' + B'CD + BCD' + AD. This is the standard two-level NAND–NAND form of a sum of products.

(d) A static hazard is a brief incorrect output pulse when a single input changes and the output should stay constant. It is caused by signals reaching the output through paths with different delays. A static-1 hazard occurs when two adjacent 1-cells are covered by different product terms that do not overlap. For the change 0011 → 1011 only A changes, and F should stay at 1, because 0011 is a valid 1 and 1011 is a don't-care that the design treats as 1 (it lies in both AD and B'CD). Both cells are covered by the single term B'CD, which does not depend on A, so that term stays at 1 throughout and F cannot glitch: there is no hazard for this transition. In normal BCD operation the input 1011 never occurs, so the question is mainly a check of the method.

questions.q:
A small microprocessor system has a 16-bit address bus and an 8-bit data bus. It contains a 16K × 8 ROM, an 8K × 8 RAM and an output port.
(a) State how many address lines each memory chip needs, and explain the roles of the address bus, data bus, chip-select and output-enable signals. [5]
(b) The ROM is to occupy 0000–3FFF and the RAM 4000–5FFF. Using full decoding, write the chip-select (active-low) logic for each in terms of the upper address lines. [6]
(c) A designer proposes to select the RAM using only A14 = 1. Explain the consequences. [3]
(d) A PIC12F675 running at 4 MHz executes: MOVLW D'200' / MOVWF C / LOOP DECFSZ C,F / GOTO LOOP. Calculate the time taken, and explain how you would extend the delay to about 0.1 s. [6]
markScheme: (a) ROM 14 lines (2¹⁴ = 16384), RAM 13 lines (2¹³ = 8192)
(a) Address bus selects location (from CPU); data bus bidirectional carries values; CS' enables the chip; OE' enables its tri-state outputs onto the bus during reads
(c) RAM selected for every address with A14 = 1: appears in 4000–7FFF and C000–FFFF (aliases) and clashes with any device placed there
(d) Cycles = 3N + 1 = 601; 1 µs per cycle → 601 µs
(d) Nested loop: outer counter M repeating the inner loop; total ≈ M × (inner + overhead ≈ 606 cycles); M ≈ 165 for 0.1 s with N = 200, or tune N and M
questions.modelAnswer:
(a) The 16K × 8 ROM has 16 384 = 2¹⁴ locations, so it needs 14 address lines (A13–A0). The 8K × 8 RAM has 8192 = 2¹³ locations, so it needs 13 address lines (A12–A0). The address bus is driven by the processor and identifies the location being accessed. The data bus is bidirectional and carries the byte being read or written. The chip-select (CS') input, usually active-low, enables a particular device; it is generated by the address decoder from the upper address lines. Output-enable (OE') allows the selected device to drive its tri-state data outputs onto the bus during a read; at all other times the outputs are high-impedance so they do not contend with other devices.

(b) ROM, 0000–3FFF: 0000 = 0000 0000 0000 0000 and 3FFF = 0011 1111 1111 1111, so A15 = 0 and A14 = 0 throughout, with A13–A0 going to the ROM. It is selected when A15'·A14' = 1, so CS'ROM = (A15'·A14')' = A15 + A14 (a two-input OR, or a NOR followed by an inverter).
RAM, 4000–5FFF: 4000 = 0100 0000 0000 0000 and 5FFF = 0101 1111 1111 1111, so A15 = 0, A14 = 1, A13 = 0, with A12–A0 going to the RAM. CS'RAM = (A15'·A14·A13')' = A15 + A14' + A13.
Check: an address such as 6000 (A13 = 1) selects neither device, as required by full decoding.

(c) If the RAM is selected whenever A14 = 1, it responds to every address of the form x1xx..., that is 4000–7FFF and C000–FFFF. A13 and A15 are not decoded, so the 8K RAM appears four times (twice within 4000–7FFF, since A13 is ignored, and twice more in C000–FFFF). The logic is simpler, but the address space is wasted and no other device (for example the output port) can be placed in those ranges without causing bus contention.

(d) Each instruction cycle is four clock periods, i.e. 1 µs at 4 MHz. MOVLW and MOVWF take 1 cycle each. For N = 200, the DECFSZ/GOTO pair runs 199 times at 1 + 2 = 3 cycles, and the final DECFSZ takes 2 cycles because it skips. Total = 2 + 3 × 199 + 2 = 601 cycles = 601 µs. To reach about 0.1 s (100 000 µs), nest this inner loop inside an outer loop with a second counter M: each outer pass costs about 606 cycles (601 for the inner loop, 2 to reload its counter and 3 for the outer DECFSZ/GOTO). About 100 000 / 606 ≈ 165 outer passes are needed, which fits in an 8-bit counter. Precise tuning can be done by adjusting N and M and counting every cycle, including the outer loop overhead. Alternatively a hardware timer could be used.
